lesson.title: Plus, Moins, aussi
lesson.subtitle: Comparing with plus… que, moins… que, aussi… que — and the twin suppletions bon → meilleur and mauvais → pire

hook.title: Why French Never Adds '-er' to an Adjective
hook.content: English has two competing ways to compare: short Germanic adjectives add '-er' (bigger, smaller, cheaper), while long Latinate adjectives put 'more' in front (more important, more interesting). French uses the 'more / less / as' formula for EVERY adjective, short or long! 'Bigger than' is simply plus grand que ('more big than'). 'Less expensive than' is moins cher que. And 'as tall as' is aussi grand que.

footnotes.title: Why bon → meilleur is the exact twin of good → better
footnotes.content: Neither English (*gooder) nor French (*plus bon) allows 'good' to take a regular comparative! Both languages reach for a separate ancient root (suppletion): Latin bonus jumped to melior (English 'ameliorate'), giving French meilleur ('better')!

pattern.title: plus / moins / aussi + Adjective + que
pattern.content: Notice that French uses que ('than') as the second hinge across all three comparisons: plus grand que ('more big than'), moins cher que ('less expensive than'), and aussi important que ('as important as'). And when you pronounce plus before an adjective starting with a consonant (plus grand, plus cher), the final -s of plus stays silent (/ply/)!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin comparative melior ('better') and peior ('worse', English pejorative) survived directly as synthetic comparatives meilleur and pire.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: saying *plus bon for 'better'. Just as English forbids 'gooder', French forbids *plus bon — always say meilleur!

exercises.prompt: Match each comparative pattern with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: bigger / taller than, less expensive / cheaper than, as important as, better than (ameliorate), worse than
exercises.meaning: plus grand que, moins cher que, aussi important que, meilleur que (never *plus bon), pire que (pejorative)
exercises.explanation: plus, moins, and aussi all close their comparison with que ('than / as').

exercises.prompt: French meilleur ('better') shares its Latin root melior with which formal English verb meaning 'to make better'?
exercises.explanation: To ameliorate a situation is literally to make it 'better' (Latin melior → French meilleur).

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'The wine is better than the coffee'?
options: Le vin est plus bon que le café
Le vin est meilleur que le café
Le vin est meilleur comme le café
exercises.target_answer: Le vin est meilleur que le café
exercises.meaning: The wine is better than the coffee
exercises.explanation: bon becomes meilleur in comparisons, and 'than' is always que.

exercises.idea: this hotel is less expensive than the restaurant
cues: This hotel is less expensive than the restaurant → Cet hôtel est moins cher que le restaurant
exercises.target_answer: Cet hôtel est moins cher que le restaurant
exercises.meaning: This hotel is less expensive than the restaurant

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: La maison est aussi grande que l'hôtel
exercises.target_answer: La maison est aussi grande que l'hôtel
exercises.meaning: The house is as big as the hotel
cues: The house is: La maison est
as big as: aussi grande que
exercises.explanation: aussi... que means 'as... as', and grande agrees with la maison.
exercises.affirmation: You paired aussi and que with feminine grande.

summary.outcome: Build comparisons of superiority (plus… que), inferiority (moins… que), and equality (aussi… que), plus irregular meilleur and pire.

use_example.german: Le train est plus rapide et moins cher que la voiture.
use_example.english: The train is faster and cheaper than the car.

summary.takeaway: Every comparison closes with que — and 'better' is always meilleur.

foreshadow.line: Having mastered Plus, Moins, aussi, look ahead to Topic 22 (en & y), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 20 (depuis & the Perfect Split) now pays off directly inside Plus, Moins, aussi: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

plus.etymology_derivation: borrowed into English whole — plus is plus. The final s falls silent in most positions.

aussi.context_phrase: Elle est aussi grande que son frère.
aussi.context_translation: She is as tall as her brother.
aussi.etymology_derivation: Inside comparisons, aussi + adjective + que means 'as [adj] as'.

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

meilleur.etymology_derivation: Latin melior — English 'ameliorate'. bon→meilleur is good→better's twin suppletion: both languages froze an old comparative.

grand.etymology_derivation: English 'grand' came straight from French; the feminine adds a silent -e, which wakes the silent d into sound: grand /ɡʁɑ̃/ → grande /ɡʁɑ̃d/.

petit.etymology_derivation: English 'petite' is the French feminine form, borrowed whole — the masculine is petit.

bon.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus 'good' — English borrowed the word back as 'bonus', a good thing added.
